lead: An engine cannot burn its fuel perfectly every cycle. Carbon monoxide comes from a rich mixture, unburnt hydrocarbons from a flame that dies or hides, and nitrogen oxides from a flame that becomes too hot. These three engine-out gases are measured before any catalytic converter. The same trade-off controls petrol and diesel tuning, cold starts, and every emission standard.
prereq: You need Unit 3 (stages of combustion, flame quenching) and Unit 2 (mixture formation and ignition timing).

blocks.text: Every regulated gas starts from a different failure of combustion. Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colourless, odourless gas made when carbon in fuel is partly oxidised: C + ½O2 → CO. Complete oxidation gives CO2. In a spark-ignition engine, CO rises steeply when the equivalence ratio φ exceeds 1. Petrol's stoichiometric air-fuel ratio is about 14.7:1 by mass; at φ = 1.1 the charge has more fuel than the oxygen can fully burn.

blocks.where: φ is the equivalence ratio; F/A is fuel-air ratio by mass; actual is the running mixture; stoichiometric is the chemically exact mixture.

blocks.text: Two reactions adjust CO after it forms. The water-gas shift CO + H2O ⇌ CO2 + H2 removes CO when water and oxygen are available. Above about 2000 K, CO2 dissociates back as CO2 ⇌ CO + ½O2, so even a lean flame leaves a small CO floor. Cold walls freeze the shift reaction and leave more CO during warm-up.

A diesel engine runs globally lean, so engine-out CO is low. Local rich pockets, low-temperature quench and poor mixing still make some CO. CO is controlled by holding φ near 1, by air injection into the exhaust, and by the catalytic converter. The converter needs a narrow window around stoichiometric mixture to oxidise CO and hydrocarbons while reducing NOx.

sections.h3: Unburnt hydrocarbons: flame death and hiding places

blocks.text: Unburnt hydrocarbons (HC) are fuel molecules that leave the cylinder without burning. Total hydrocarbons (THC) are measured as equivalent carbon atoms, usually ppm C1 or ppm C3. Six paths matter.

items: Wall quenching: the flame cools and dies within roughly 1 mm of a cold wall. The boundary layer survives, especially with cold coolant.
Crevice volumes: the piston top land, ring grooves, and spark-plug gap hold mixture that the flame cannot enter. It leaves during expansion.
Oil-film absorption: fuel dissolves in the lubricating oil when pressure is high and returns later.
Short-circuiting: with valve overlap, fresh mixture can pass from intake to exhaust before the flame arrives.
Misfire: a cycle with no flame leaves all its fuel as HC.
Poor atomisation: a cold engine, low fuel pressure, or a wide spray makes liquid films that burn slowly.

blocks.text: Cold-start HC can be most of a petrol car's HC. In a diesel, over-lean outer spray and fuel wetting the nozzle also add HC. Spark timing that is too retarded lowers peak temperature and raises HC. HC falls as the mixture leans out, until lean misfire sets in.

sections.h3: NOx: the hot-flame gas and the trade-off

blocks.text: NOx means nitric oxide NO plus nitrogen dioxide NO2. In engine exhaust, NO is usually the larger share; NO2 is a small part that grows at light load and in diesel exhaust. Thermal NO forms from atmospheric nitrogen and oxygen in the hot burned gas.
O + N2 → NO + N; N + O2 → NO + O; N + OH → NO + H
blocks.where: N2 is nitrogen from air; O, N, OH and H are radicals in the flame; NO is nitric oxide. These three reactions are the Zeldovich mechanism.

blocks.text: The first reaction has a high activation energy, so thermal NO rises steeply above about 1800 K. It depends on peak temperature, oxygen concentration and residence time. A slightly lean mixture, φ ≈ 0.9, gives high temperature with oxygen still present; that is where NOx peaks. Richer mixtures lower temperature and oxygen, so NOx falls. Prompt NO forms in the flame front by reactions of hydrocarbon radicals with N2. It is small in most engines but matters in very rich, short flames.

NOx is reduced by lower peak temperature: retarded spark, exhaust gas recirculation (EGR), lower compression ratio, or late injection. These same changes often raise CO or HC. From rich to lean: CO and HC fall as oxygen becomes available; NOx rises to a peak near air-fuel ratio 15 and then falls as excess air cools the flame and dilutes the charge. The three-way catalyst works only in a narrow band around stoichiometric, so the engine is held there and the remaining gases are converted in the exhaust. High load raises peak temperature and NOx; cold coolant raises HC and CO.

figure.caption: Engine-out CO and HC fall as the mixture leans out, while NOx peaks just lean of stoichiometric and then falls. Notice the narrow region near 14.7:1 where a three-way catalyst can work.

spec.aria: Graph of CO, HC and NOx concentration against air-fuel ratio; CO and HC fall as the mixture leans out while NOx rises to a peak near an air-fuel ratio of 15 and then falls.

examples.question: A petrol engine passes 0.05 m³/s of dry exhaust at standard conditions, where the density of CO is 1.25 kg/m³. The NDIR analyser reads 0.4% CO by volume and brake power is 60 kW. Find the CO mass flow and the brake-specific CO in g/kWh.
steps: CO mass flow = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³/s × 1.25 kg/m³ = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ kg/s.
Convert to grams per second: 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ kg/s × 1000 g/kg = 0.25 g/s.
examples.answer: The CO mass flow is 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ kg/s (0.25 g/s), and the brake-specific CO is 15 g/kWh.
examples.check:
vol_frac = 0.4 / 100
q = 0.05
rho = 1.25
P = 60
vol_co = vol_frac * q
mass_co = vol_co * rho
g_s = mass_co * 1000
bs = g_s / P
bs_kwh = bs * 3600
print(mass_co)
print(g_s)
print(bs_kwh)

traps: Assuming NOx rises with richness because the flame gets hotter. NOx peaks slightly lean of stoichiometric, near φ ≈ 0.9, where temperature is still high and oxygen is still present.
Saying NO comes from fuel nitrogen. In ordinary petrol and diesel, thermal NO comes from N2 in the air; fuel nitrogen matters only in some special fuels.
Treating HC as only unburned fuel vapour. THC includes partially burned molecules and oil-derived species, and ppm C1 counts carbon atoms.
Using wet exhaust volume when the analyser reads dry gas. Percent CO is on a dry basis, so water must be removed before the NDIR measurement.

quiz.a: φ = (F/A)actual ÷ (F/A)stoichiometric, where F/A is fuel-air ratio by mass.

quiz.q: Name two crevice volumes that trap unburnt mixture.
quiz.a: Piston top land and ring grooves; also spark-plug gap or valve seats.

quiz.q: Why does wall quenching produce unburnt hydrocarbons?
quiz.a: The flame loses heat to the cold wall and dies within about 1 mm, leaving a boundary layer of unburned mixture that exits during exhaust.

quiz.q: Why does NOx peak slightly lean of stoichiometric instead of at the richest or hottest point?
quiz.a: Lean enough for oxygen to remain, but still hot enough for the Zeldovich reactions; richer mixtures lack oxygen and leaner mixtures are cooler.

quiz.q: Dry exhaust flow is 0.02 m³/s, CO reads 0.8% by volume, CO density is 1.25 kg/m³, and brake power is 30 kW. Find brake-specific CO in g/kWh.
quiz.a: CO volume flow = 0.008 × 0.02 = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ m³/s; mass flow = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ × 1.25 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg/s = 0.2 g/s; brake-specific = 0.2 ÷ 30 × 3600 = 24 g/kWh.

quiz.q: A technician advances spark timing to reduce HC. Explain the likely effect on NOx and CO.
quiz.a: Advancing timing raises peak temperature and pressure, so NOx usually rises. CO may fall if combustion is more complete, but knock and higher NOx limit the advance; the three gases move together, not one at a time.

quiz.q: Why does a three-way catalyst need the mixture held near φ = 1, and what happens outside that window?
quiz.a: Near stoichiometric the catalyst can oxidise CO and HC while reducing NOx. Lean mixture leaves NOx unconverted; rich mixture leaves CO and HC unconverted.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production engines now combine close-coupled catalysts, wide-band oxygen sensors and high-pressure EGR to hold the trade-off inside a narrow window. Research on low-temperature combustion tries to stay below the NOx formation temperature while premixing enough to avoid soot. Biofuels change the oxygen and nitrogen content of the fuel, so their engine-out CO and NOx are not simply the petrol values. Search next for Zeldovich mechanism, exhaust gas recirculation, and three-way catalyst window.
